title: Custodian concise asks and technical sales lattice
body:
Purpose: a compact playbook for technical sellers and solution engineers to surface the minimal (and sufficient) asks custodial stakeholders need to sign off on private (VPC / on-prem) inference. Focus: regulated workloads + control plane language + succinct rebuttals to common skeptic objections.

Why this exists (context + problem):
- Field feedback: long playbooks confuse buyers; security teams want a crisp checklist — what they need from us vs what they must own.
- We lose momentum in >2 week procurement stretches when asks feel vague or slide-deck-y.
- Need a single-page narrative per stakeholder (CISO/Audit, InfraOps, Platform Eng, Legal/Privacy) + a technical lattice that maps claims -> evidence -> verification step.

Intended usage: quick-reference for SEs during discovery calls and pilot scoping. Also meant to be copy-paste into email threads and SOW bullets.

One-line positioning (for technical stakeholders):
"Redwood Private gives you a customer-controlled data plane with a lock-step control plane integration: we operate the orchestrator while you retain cryptographic custody and audit visibility—minimal changes to your network and full auditability for regulated workflows."

Custodian asks (minimal, with one-sentence rationale each):
1) Network boundary and egress policy (Rationale: ensures no hidden exfiltration from inference nodes)
   - Ask: A CI/CD accessible bastion subnet / peered VPC and documented egress ACLs.
   - SE script snippet: "Can you confirm the subnet we will peer to and any IP allowlists? For the pilot we only need TLS outbound to our control-plane endpoints (or a private endpoint if on-prem)."

2) Key custody scope (Rationale: who can access model encryption keys and audit logs)
   - Ask: KMS tenant + rotation policy; if using customer HSM provide connector details.
   - SE script: "Is your KMS HSM available to our connector, or do you prefer we ship a key-wrapping envelope?"

3) Audit surface and log retention (Rationale: demonstrate traceability for every inference request)
   - Ask: Retention window for request/response hashes, access logs, and Syslog/SIEM forwarding endpoint.
   - Evidence we provide: request id tagging, optional request hashing (non-sensitive), sigchain for admin actions.

4) Data residency & model artifacts policy (Rationale: where weights and cached KV live matters for sovereignty rules)
   - Ask: Acceptable storage locations for model cache + whether model artifacts must be airgapped.
   - Note: If airgap required, flag for infra/prof services scoping.

5) Operator privilege model (Rationale: least privilege for ops -> auditability + trust)
   - Ask: RBAC mapping for their identity provider and list of emergency escalation contacts.
   - SE script: "Can we map Redwood platform roles to an existing SAML/OIDC group, and provide a test user for role verification?"

Technical lattice (claims -> required artifact -> verification method):
- Claim: "Control plane cannot read inference payloads."
  - Artifact: KMS rotation logs, network flow diagram, TLS mTLS handshake details.
  - Verification: Customer test with hashed payload verification + SIEM correlation.

- Claim: "Model weights never leave customer storage when requested."
  - Artifact: S3/VPC endpoint config + signed download URLs / hash manifest.
  - Verification: Hash reconciliation + storage ACL review.

- Claim: "Operator actions are auditable and require customer approval for critical changes."
  - Artifact: Admin action audit trail, change approval workflow screenshot.
  - Verification: Walkthrough + simulated rollback test.

Buyer objection bank (concise rebuttals):
- Objection: "You still control the control plane — we can't trust you."
  - Rebuttal: "We operate an orchestration control plane but we have no key material and all sensitive I/O stays on your network. Think of Redwood like a scheduler with signed manifests; we never hold plaintext inference inputs. Let's schedule a short live demo where we show the mTLS handshake and a payload hash verification so your security team can validate."

- Objection: "This looks like a managed service — we need full on-prem ownership."
  - Rebuttal: "We support an on-prem private control plane package as an optional engagement (prof services + license). For most regulated pilots customers prefer our managed control plane but with KMS/HSM in their environment; we can flip to fully self-managed on longer-term contracts."

- Objection: "What about model leakage via caching or logs?"
  - Rebuttal: "We provide configurable KV cache TTLs, cache encryption at rest with customer keys, and an option to disable caching entirely for high-risk endpoints. We can demonstrate a cache-disabled mode during pilot."

- Objection: "How will you handle subpoenas or requests for data?"
  - Rebuttal: "We surface all legal requests and have a documented escalation path. When keys and logs are customer-held, the practical impact is the same as other vendor connectors — your legal team can request our transparency report and we can include contractual SLAs around notice where permitted by law."

Competitor deltas (short and tactical for field):
- Vendor A: heavy on self-host but slow to patch; delta: Redwood offers rapid upstream kernel and quantization patches via a managed feed plus optional self-host bundle.
- Vendor B: advertises control-plane export but has coarse-grained RBAC; delta: Redwood supports fine-grained RBAC + SAML group sync and per-route audit hooks.
- Cloud native endpoints (big cloud): advantage in default compliance certs; delta: Redwood emphasizes model-level observability, deterministic fallbacks, and lower per-token economics for sustained inference.

Quick scripts (30–60s):
- CISO intro (email snippet):
  "Hi [CISO],
  quick note: our pilot request is intentionally narrow — we only need network peering, KMS access for key wrapping, and a log sink. We can run an auditable smoke test where no plaintext leaves your VPC and you can validate each event in your SIEM. If desirable, we can propose an on-prem control plane alternative in the contract. Happy to set up a 30-min demo with your infra/security lead."

- InfraOps slack opener (discovery):
  "hey — SE here. For the pilot can you confirm whether we should use VPC peering or PrivateLink? Also curious about any egress restrictions so we can scope NAT/Proxy configs."

Open questions / escalation points (TODOs):
- Define standard test harness for "no-plaintext" verification (work with applied-ml to build reproducible script).
- Legal to propose contract paragraph for notice handling of legal process (tie to control plane vs data plane custody).
- Eng: produce an ODM (operator duty matrix) doc mapping actions that require customer approval.

Notes to self / field tips:
- Keep the ask list minimal during first outreach; escalate to full lattice only after SI and infra buy-in.
- Use the word "custody" deliberately — custodians care about keys, not about who runs the orchestrator.
- Avoid over-promising about on-prem packaging timeline; be explicit about prof services lead time.

Next steps (for this doc):
- Fold feedback from SEs in next week (target: 2026-02-25).
- Create a one-page PDF cheat sheet for AE/SDR use.
- Ship pilot verification script to solutions repo and link in Confluence.

References / helpful links:
- Pilot checklist (confluence): https://confluence.redwood.example/display/INF/Private+Pilot+Checklist
- Security architecture diagram (internal): share on request

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: initial capture after pilot with fintech prospect.
- 2026-01-09: added technical lattice and quick scripts.
- 2026-02-18: updated competitor deltas and TODOs after SE sync.

Unresolved: what to do for governments with stricter data export rules — need legal + enterprise sales pattern library.

End of doc.
